questions.question: What is the String pool in Java?
questions.title: String Pool
questions.direct_answer: The String pool is a cache in the JVM heap where String literals are stored and reused, so identical literals share the same object.

beats.content: The String pool is a cache inside the JVM heap. When you write String a = "hello" in five different places, the JVM doesn't create five objects. It creates one "hello" in the pool and all five variables point to it.

content: String literals automatically go through the pool — reuse happens transparently
new String("hello") bypasses the pool and always creates a fresh heap object
"hello" == "hello" returns true because both point to the same pooled object
In Java 6, the pool lived in PermGen — a fixed-size area; heavy interning caused OutOfMemoryError
In Java 7+, the pool moved to the regular heap — it can grow and strings in it can be garbage collected

beats.content: intern() lets you manually bring a String into the pool. You rarely need it in normal code, but it's used when loading millions of duplicate strings from files or databases to save memory.

sections.hook: Java doesn't create a new String object every time you write a literal. The pool ensures identical literals share one object. Here's how.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So the String pool — also called the String intern pool — is a special area in the JVM heap where String literals are stored. The idea is that if you write `String a = "hello"` in five different places, the JVM doesn't create five separate objects. It creates one 'hello' object in the pool and all five variables point to the same object.

This is why `"hello" == "hello"` returns true in Java — both references point to the same pooled object. But `new String("hello") == new String("hello")` returns false, because you're explicitly asking Java to bypass the pool and create new heap objects.

In Java 6 and earlier, the pool lived in PermGen which had limited size. In Java 7+, it was moved to the regular heap, so it can grow as needed and objects in it can be garbage collected.

You can also manually add a String to the pool using `intern()` — `s.intern()` checks if an equal string is in the pool; if yes it returns that pooled reference, if not it adds s to the pool. This is rarely needed in practice but sometimes used in memory-critical code.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Literals reuse same object → memory savings
"hello" == "hello" is true (same pool object)
new String("hello") bypasses the pool
Java 7+: pool lives in heap (not PermGen), can be GC'd
intern() manually adds/retrieves from pool

questions.question: What is the difference between String s = "hello" and String s = new String("hello")?
questions.title: String Literal vs new String()
questions.direct_answer: String literal uses the pool (reuses existing object if present), while new String() always creates a new heap object outside the pool.

beats.content: String s = "hello" goes through the pool. If "hello" already exists there, s gets that existing object. String s = new String("hello") skips the pool entirely and always creates a fresh object on the heap.
The takeaway: content equality is all that matters in practice, and .equals() gives you that reliably regardless of whether objects came from the pool or not. Never use == to compare String content.

sections.hook: Two ways to get a String with the same content — but == gives different results for each. Here's the memory picture.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So when you write `String s = "hello"`, Java checks the string pool first. If 'hello' is already there, s gets a reference to that existing object. If not, Java creates 'hello' in the pool and s points to it.

When you write `String s = new String("hello")`, Java always creates a fresh object on the heap, outside the pool. Even if 'hello' already exists in the pool, you still get a new separate object.

This is why:
```java
String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
System.out.println(a == b);  // true — same pool object

String c = new String("hello");
String d = new String("hello");
System.out.println(c == d);  // false — different heap objects
System.out.println(a == c);  // false — pool vs heap

System.out.println(a.equals(c));  // true — same content
```

The practical lesson: always use .equals() to compare String content. Never use == unless you specifically want reference equality, which is almost never the case with Strings.

beats.content: intern() is a manual handle into the String pool. Calling s.intern() asks Java: is there already an equal string in the pool? If yes, return that pooled reference. If no, add this string to the pool and return it.

content: Main use case: deduplication when reading millions of strings from external sources
Example: reading city names from a CSV — "Mumbai" appears 50,000 times; intern() makes them all point to one object
intern() does not modify the original string — it returns a (possibly different) reference

sections.hook: intern() is the manual lever for the String pool. You won't need it often — but knowing when it helps shows real JVM depth.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So intern() is a way to manually bring a String into the pool. When you call s.intern(), Java checks: is there already a String in the pool that equals s? If yes, it returns that pooled reference. If no, it adds s to the pool and returns it.

The main use case is when you're reading millions of strings from an external source — like reading the same city names from a CSV file — and you want to deduplicate them in memory. Without intern(), each readLine() creates a separate String object even if the content is identical. With intern(), all 'Mumbai' strings point to the same pool object.

In normal application code you almost never need intern() because you control string creation. But it comes up in certain high-throughput data processing scenarios. Java's String.intern() can actually be slow due to native JNI overhead, so in performance-critical code people sometimes use a `Map<String,String>` as a manual pool instead.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Returns pooled version of the string
Adds to pool if not present
Use case: deduplicating many identical strings from external data
Rarely needed in normal code
Can be slow (native call) — manual HashMap pool sometimes faster

questions.question: Can strings in the String pool be garbage collected?
questions.title: String Pool and GC
questions.direct_answer: Yes — since Java 7, the pool lives in the heap and unreferenced pool strings can be garbage collected, unlike Java 6 where the pool was in PermGen.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying pool strings are permanent — true only for Java 6 PermGen

beats.content: Yes, they can — but only since Java 7. Before that, the answer was no, and the consequence was serious.

content: Java 6: pool lived in PermGen — fixed size, not subject to normal GC, heavy interning caused OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space
Java 7+: pool moved to the regular heap — subject to normal GC, can grow dynamically
A pool string is GC-eligible once no live references point to it
Interning millions of strings is now safer, though it still has memory and performance cost

sections.hook: Pool strings used to be permanent. Java 7 changed that — and it fixed a real production OOM problem.

questions.question: What happens internally when you concatenate strings with the + operator?
questions.title: String + Operator Compilation
questions.direct_answer: The compiler converts simple + concatenation to StringBuilder — but in loops it creates a new StringBuilder per iteration, not one shared instance.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the compiler always optimizes + to be as fast as explicit StringBuilder
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain exactly why loops defeat the optimization — each iteration is a separate expression

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: For a simple one-liner like "a" + "b" + "c", the Java compiler rewrites it to new StringBuilder().append("a").append("b").append("c").toString() — no problem. But this optimization has a hard limit.

content: In a loop, each iteration is a separate expression — the compiler creates a new StringBuilder per iteration
That means N loop iterations = N StringBuilder objects created and discarded
The compiler cannot merge StringBuilder across loop boundaries
Explicit StringBuilder.append() in a loop solves this — one object, N appends, one toString() at the end
Java 9+ uses invokedynamic for even more efficient literal concat — but the loop problem remains

sections.hook: The compiler optimizes String + behind the scenes. But it hits a wall at loop boundaries — and that's where you have to step in manually.

content: 'a' + 'b' + 'c' compiles to: new StringBuilder().append('a').append('b').append('c').toString()
Loop body: new StringBuilder created each iteration = N objects total

Compiler optimizes single-expression + but NOT across loop boundaries
Always use StringBuilder.append() manually in loops
